<result>**Digest: AI presales/RFP landscape (searches run 2026-10-01; many sources are vendor-authored)**

**1. Commercial tools**
- Category split: library-based incumbents (Loopio, Responsive, Qvidian) versus AI-native or "agentic" entrants (Inventive, Arphie, Tribble, AutogenAI, Thalamus). Responsive added a ChatGPT integration in April 2026. Comparison pages are mostly written by competitors, so the scores are self-interested. https://autogenai.com/blog/best-ai-proposal-software-2026/ and https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/loopio-alternatives
- Almost all of them do retrieval, grounded drafting, source citations, questionnaire automation and workflow. AutogenAI adds a "TRACE" readiness score for responses.
- Inventive claims "multi-agent" use, and Thalamus claims 20+ agents for complex or government RFPs. These agents appear to split drafting and QA work. I found no evidence of agents with conflicting positions on timeline or cost, negotiation between agents, or delivery estimation. https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/tribble-ai-review-pricing-features-reviews
- Vivun's "Ava" is an AI sales engineer. It does meeting prep, live answers and follow-up material, built on knowledge graphs. This is the closest thing to presales rather than RFP tooling. Its claim of a "37% increase in technical win rates" comes from a vendor-commissioned survey (UserEvidence), so treat it as marketing. https://saastr.com/ai-app-of-the-week-vivun-the-ai-sales-engineer-that-actually-does-the-work/
- Feasibility, scope, delivery-estimate or cross-functional conflict detection: nothing found. This is a gap in what I could see, not proof that no vendor does it.

**2. Pain evidence**
- Loopio's 2025 benchmark (vendor report, 1,500+ teams): about 25 hours per RFP (down from 30), average win rate 45% (up from 43%). Self-reported. https://loopio.com/blog/rfp-statistics-win-rates
- Consensus 2025 Sales Engineering Workload Report (600+ presales professionals): about 56% of SE time goes to direct sales work. https://goconsensus.com/research/2025-sales-engineering-compensation-workload-report
- Claims that SEs spend 30â€“50% of time on retrieval and assembly, or that over 40% of time on questionnaires cuts deal engagement by 30%, come from vendor blogs. Treat them as weak. The RFP share of SE time is estimated at 5â€“15% on average, but it arrives in bursts. https://www.sifthub.io/blog/presales-metrics-2026
- I found no independent, peer-reviewed win-rate uplift data for any of these tools.

**3. Multi-agent patterns**
- MAST taxonomy (Berkeley, NeurIPS 2025): 14 failure modes across 7 frameworks and 200+ tasks, grouped as specification issues, inter-agent misalignment and weak verification. Gains over single-agent or best-of-N baselines are often minimal. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657
- Anthropic's research system (orchestrator plus workers) beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal eval. It used about 15x the tokens of a normal chat, and token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance. It works best when tasks decompose into parallel, independent threads. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
- I did not retrieve sources on production "debate" or negotiation specifically. Evidence for negotiation loops is thin. Cognition's "don't build multi-agents" essay is a known counterpoint, but I did not fetch it.

**4. Warehouse automation / intralogistics**
- AutoStore's Grid Designer is a browser-based 3D designer with live simulation. It includes SmartDesigner recommendations and claims 99%+ performance prediction accuracy (vendor claim). Integrators use it to co-design with clients. There is also a WMS SDK simulator. https://autostoresystem.com/insights/discover-grid-designer-advanced-3d-warehouse-design-simulation
- I found no AI presales or proposal agents specific to intralogistics. Evidence here is thin.

**Implications for the brief**
1. **Commoditised:** RFP Q&A retrieval, drafting with citations, and security questionnaires. Don't build or pitch this as the differentiator. Buy it or integrate it.
2. **White space:** feasibility, delivery estimate and commercial reconciliation across specialist agents, with a decision trace. I found no competitor doing this, but absence from search is not proof.
3. **Domain angle:** in intralogistics, the vendor design and simulation tools (e.g. Grid Designer) look like the credible source of feasibility truth. The platform should call those tools and not have the model guess performance.
4. **Risk:** negotiation rounds multiply cost (the ~15x token precedent) and bring the MAST failure modes. Conflict detection with structured outputs and a human decision may beat free-form agent debate. Validate that against a single-agent baseline.
5. **Claims discipline:** the ROI numbers (25 hours per RFP, 45% win rate, +37%) all come from vendors. Baseline your own team's effort before promising anything.</result>

<result>**Digest as of 2026-10-01.** I did a limited number of fetches. The fetch tool returns summaries from a small model, so treat unconfirmed items as unverified.

**Ollama and tooling**

| Item | Finding | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Latest stable | v0.35.0, 2026-09-28. Recent notes include v0.34.4, "single-pass structured outputs on thinking models". I could not cross-check the release notes beyond the listing. | [github.com/ollama/ollama/releases](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases) |
| Structured outputs | `format` accepts a JSON schema, or `"json"`. Docs advise also putting the schema in the prompt and using a low temperature. Ollama Cloud lacks it; local is fine. | [docs.ollama.com/capabilities/structured-outputs](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/structured-outputs) |
| OpenAI-compatible API | Yes, including `response_format`. | same page |
| Tool calling | Yes. Models carry a "tools" tag in the library. | [ollama.com/library](https://ollama.com/library?sort=popular) |
| Concurrency | `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` per model, docs default 1. A benchmark write-up says 4 (docs say 1, so unconfirmed). `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS` defaults to 3 per GPU (3 on CPU). `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE` is 512, `KEEP_ALIVE` is 5m, and the default context is 4096 (`OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`). Flash attention is on automatically where supported. `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0` roughly halves KV memory. Parallel slots multiply KV memory. | [docs.ollama.com/faq](https://docs.ollama.com/faq) |
| Docker + GPU | I did not fetch the Docker docs. From general knowledge: `ollama/ollama` image, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, `--gpus=all`. **Unconfirmed.** | none |
| langchain-ollama | v1.1.0, 2026-04-07, Python >=3.10. A newer release may exist, since PyPI was only summarised. | [pypi.org/project/langchain-ollama](https://pypi.org/pypi/langchain-ollama/json) |

I found no evidence on how reliable `with_structured_output` on `ChatOllama` is. It should route through Ollama's `format` grammar, which is constrained decoding, so I expect it to be good. Test it with your schemas, and keep a Pydantic validate-and-retry fallback.

**Models**

| Model | Sizes and VRAM | Context | Licence | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3.8 (newest, vision, tools, thinking) | 27B file is 18 GB, so about 22-24 GB with KV | 256K | Not stated on the page. Check before commercial use. | [library/qwen3.8](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3.8) |
| gpt-oss | 20b is 14 GB (16 GB RAM or VRAM); 120b is 65 GB (one 80 GB GPU). Reasoning effort is selectable. | 128K | Apache 2.0, commercial use OK | [library/gpt-oss](https://ollama.com/library/gpt-oss) |
| granite4.2 | 3B / 8B / 30B, tools | Not confirmed | Not confirmed (earlier Granite releases were Apache 2.0) | [library](https://ollama.com/library?sort=popular) |
| gemma3 | 270M-27B, vision | Not confirmed | Gemma terms, not OSI | library |
| llama3.1 | 8B / 70B / 405B | 128K | Llama community licence | library |
| deepseek-r1 | 1.5B-671B distills | Not confirmed | Not confirmed | library |

I could not confirm Llama 4, Mistral or Gemma 4 availability in Ollama, or any licences except gpt-oss. My suggested fit by task:
- **(a) Extraction/JSON:** qwen3.8:27b, or gpt-oss:20b if you want a cheaper option.
- **(b) Reasoning:** gpt-oss:20b at medium or high effort, or qwen3.8 with thinking on.
- **(c) Long context:** qwen3.8 (256K) or gpt-oss (128K). KV cache is the real limit, so set `num_ctx` explicitly (50 pages is about 40-60K tokens).

**Embeddings** ([ollama.com/search?c=embedding](https://ollama.com/search?c=embedding))

| Model | Size | Multilingual |
|---|---|---|
| qwen3-embedding | 0.6b / 4b / 8b | Yes (dims not verified) |
| bge-m3 | 567M | Yes |
| embeddinggemma | 300M | Yes |
| nomic-embed-text-v2-moe | not listed | Yes |
| nomic-embed-text | not listed | English-focused |
| mxbai-embed-large | 335M | English-focused |

I did not verify dimensions or licences. From memory, bge-m3 is 1024-dim and nomic-embed-text is 768-dim.

**Speed and cost (secondary sources, rough)**
- **CPU-only:** about 5-10 tok/s on small models (3-4B) ([source](https://use-apify.com/docs/self-hosted/ai/ollama)). An 8B model is slower, and 27-30B dense is unusable.
- **RTX 4090:** about 120-145 tok/s for an 8B Q4 ([source](https://markaicode.com/benchmarks/ollama-qwen-3-rtx-4090-throughput-benchmark/)).
- **L40S:** the 50-80 tok/s figure for an 8B looks low and is unconfirmed.
- **Qwen3 30B-A3B on Ollama:** an open GitHub issue reports it running slower than expected on a 4090.
- **70B-class:** I have no verified numbers. It needs about 40 GB VRAM at Q4.
- **Concurrency:** Ollama throughput plateaus under load. Red Hat measured about 41 tok/s for Ollama against about 793 tok/s for vLLM at high concurrency on an A100 ([markaicode summary](https://markaicode.com/benchmarks/tool-throughput-benchmark/)). Single-request latency is similar.

**EU GPU prices**

| Provider | Price | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Hetzner GEX44 (RTX 4000-class) | â‚¬184/month plus â‚¬79 setup | [Effloow](https://effloow.com/articles/hetzner-cloud-ai-gpu-server-guide-2026) |
| Hetzner GEX131 | launched at â‚¬889/month; one source says â‚¬1,197 plus â‚¬599 setup by Sep 2026 | [source](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/17339/contabo-launches-gpu-vps-999-euros-hetzner-gex131) |
| Scaleway L4 | about $0.91/hour, so about $660/month if always on | [computeprices](https://computeprices.com/providers/scaleway/gpus/l4) |
| Scaleway L40S | about â‚¬1.40/hour, so about â‚¬1,000/month | [computeprices](https://computeprices.com/providers/scaleway/gpus/l40s) |
| OVH L4 | about $0.86/hour | [sparecores](https://sparecores.com/server/ovh/l4-90) |
| OVH L40S | about $1.80/hour | [vpsbenchmarks](https://www.vpsbenchmarks.com/gpu_plans/ovhcloud/l40s-360) |
| RunPod (NL/RO) | 4090 about $0.34-0.69/hour (not a firm price) | search result |

I could not confirm Lambda or Vultr EU pricing. Hourly rates run 24/7 add up to more than a Hetzner dedicated box.

**Alternatives:** vLLM scales much better under concurrency (the 3x to 29x figures above come from secondary benchmarks). I did not research llama.cpp server or SGLang. Ollama becomes the bottleneck when you sustain more than about 4-8 concurrent agent calls.

**Implications**
- **Minimum viable hardware:** one GPU with at least 24 GB VRAM (4090/L4-class, or Hetzner GEX44 at 20 GB for a ~20B model). CPU-only is not viable for dozens of calls per job on 8B+ models, and is only workable for embeddings and a ~3B model.
- **Default pair:** `gpt-oss:20b` (Apache 2.0, 14 GB, structured output and tools) for chat, plus `bge-m3` or `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` for embeddings. Upgrade to `qwen3.8:27b` once its licence is checked and you have 24 GB or more.
- **Risks:**
  - Ollama's default 4096 context silently truncates long docs, so set `num_ctx`.
  - Parallel slots multiply VRAM use.
  - Several results (Qwen3.8, v0.35) come from page summaries only, so verify them directly.
  - GPU prices are rising.
  - Plan a vLLM migration path.</result>

One focused revision pass would fix most of it: add rows to State Patterns and Component Patterns, plus a status vocabulary table. I did not edit the spines.

| # | Section | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Flow coverage | adequate |

**Findings by severity:** 0 critical, 10 high, 22 medium, 16 low (48 total).

Mechanically, every `{token}` reference resolves, every colour has a light and dark pair, all three source paths resolve, and the DESIGN.md section order matches the spec.

**Top 5 findings:**
1. **[high]** The submit gate and the Baseline gate are mixed up. The Submission Blockers list counts "pending Review" as a blocker to submitting, but reviews happen after submission. So Flow 1 would show a blocker right after it reads "0 blockers", and setting the Baseline has no flow, state or blocked treatment (EXPERIENCE.md L75, L179; FR-62, AD-27).
2. **[high]** The status-pill vocabulary is a dangling reference. DESIGN.md L170 says pills follow "EXPERIENCE.md statuses", but EXPERIENCE.md has no such table, so none of the 9 architecture state machines map to a label, icon or colour.
3. **[high]** The review decisions in AD-28 have no outcome for the author. Nothing says what the presales engineer sees or does after a reject, request for evidence, request for an alternative, or escalation. Separately, Flow 2 has the reviewer confirm which Assessments to rerun after a Challenge, but FR-38 says the presales engineer confirms it.
4. **[high]** Key states are missing: most of the Estimate Version lifecycle (in review, approved, rejected, superseded), any marker showing which version is the Baseline, what the Estimate tab shows before the first version exists, and what happens when a Source upload is rejected or fails to parse.
5. **[high]** No contrast targets are stated anywhere. The light-mode Gap amber `#D97706` is 3.19:1 on white, which fails WCAG AA (needs 4.5:1) for the small count text in the gap badges. That is a risk against NFR-7.

Other notable gaps:
- UJ-4 (Scenarios, R3) has no Key Flow.
- Seven components have behaviour rows but no visual spec, including the Gap card, Conflict view and Review panel.
- There is no way to dismiss a Gap with a reason.
- The Knowledge and Admin surfaces are a single IA row each.
- Single-GPU queuing means runs can sit queued, but there is no "queued" run state.

The Agent Registry defines which agents are available and what each agent is authorized to do.

- Agents must have unique IDs.
- Disabled agents must not receive new tasks.
- Agent versions must be recorded.
- Tool permissions must be validated before execution.
- The orchestrator must select agents based on capabilities.
- Agent configuration changes must be auditable.
- Incompatible agent versions must be rejected.

## 15.1 Purpose

Resolve conflicts through structured, bounded negotiation.

## 15.2 Negotiation Protocol

### Round 1 â€” Independent Positions

Each agent submits its recommendation, evidence, constraints, and assumptions.

### Round 2 â€” Conflict Detection

The system identifies incompatible positions.

### Round 3 â€” Challenge

Agents evaluate the assumptions behind conflicting recommendations.

### Round 4 â€” Alternatives

Agents propose alternative scenarios.

### Round 5 â€” Trade-Off Analysis

The system compares feasibility, cost, timeline, risk, and dependencies.

### Round 6 â€” Consensus Evaluation

The system determines whether a sufficiently supported decision can be produced.

### Round 7 â€” Critic Review

An independent Critic evaluates the proposed consensus.

### Round 8 â€” Escalation

Unresolved conflicts are sent to a human reviewer.

## 15.3 Negotiation Limits

The system must enforce:

- Configurable maximum rounds.
- Configurable execution timeout.
- Maximum model-call budget.
- Maximum token budget.
- Maximum tool-call budget.
- Escalation when no acceptable consensus is reached.

  - A new Estimate Version carries Assumptions and Risks forward explicitly.
